extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, writers, literary critics, and students of culture
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative distinctions about 'culture' (what counts as real culture), the contrast between Hebraism and Hellenism, and social aims such as equality and manners — useful for writers, critics, and cultural commentators seeking standards for cultural writing and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture should humanize and diffuse the best knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture 'seeks to do away with classes; to make the best that has been thought and known in the world current everywhere; to make all men live in an atmosphere of sweetness and light, where they may use ideas...freely,--nourished, and not bound by them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'teach down' or confine the best knowledge to a clique. Aim to divest knowledge of the harsh, uncouth, difficult, abstract, professional, exclusive aspects so it becomes efficient outside the cultivated circle. Examples of this humanizing diffusion include Abelard, Lessing, and Herder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of culture: 'real' thought and beauty required
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture requires 'real thought and real beauty; real sweetness and real light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality is not mere appearance or popular adaptation; the thought and beauty offered must be genuine. Avoid counterfeit or merely adapted 'intellectual food' for the masses that lacks authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture must not indoctrinate with ready-made judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture 'does not try to teach down to the level of inferior classes; it does not try to win them for this or that sect of its own, with ready-made judgments and watchwords.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include ordinary popular literature framed to fit presumed mass tastes and religious/political organs that 'indoctrinate' rather than cultivate. Good cultural writing opens minds rather than imposes slogans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Men of culture are apostles of equality
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'social idea' of culture: the men of culture 'have had a passion for diffusing...the best knowledge...to humanize it, to make it efficient outside the clique of the cultivated', acting as 'true apostles of equality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural work should promote social leveling in terms of access to ideas and manners; cultural effort is measured by its diffusion and humanizing effect across society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between doing and thinking (Hebraism vs Hellenism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two rival forces: Hebraism (preference for doing, conduct, obedience, strictness of conscience) and Hellenism (preference for knowing, seeing things as they are, spontaneity of consciousness). 'Between these two points of influence moves our world...it ought to be...evenly and happily balanced between them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate intellectual or moral positions by whether they over-emphasize action at the expense of understanding or vice versa. Cultural health requires alternation and balance; neither pole should be treated as the whole law of human development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hellenism values clear intelligence and apprehending reality
rubrics_metrics.description: Hellenism's 'uppermost idea...is to see things as they really are' and it prizes 'spontaneity of consciousness' and intellectual vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works or cultural currents should be assessed for intellectual clarity, pursuit of truth, love of beauty, and capacity to reveal reality and reason; Hellenic strength is the cultivation of intellect and aesthetic perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hebraism values conduct, obedience, and self-conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: Hebraism's 'uppermost idea...is conduct and obedience' with emphasis on moral strictness: 'the discipline of the Old Testament may be summed up as a discipline teaching us to abhor and flee from sin; the discipline of the New Testament...teaching us to die to it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cultural or literary works for moral earnestness, seriousness about sin and self-discipline, and their capacity to foster obedience and character-forming habits; Hebraic strength is moral rigor and will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge human difficulties (sin) as real obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Sin...fills the whole scene' in Hebraism; culture that ignores such obstacles is premature or inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good cultural/moral writing must reckon with human weakness and the difficulty of moral attainment; superficial optimism that ignores sin is critiqued as unsound for its moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternation and historical balance are necessary for progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Human spirit proceeds 'by alternations of Hebraism and Hellenism...each of these two forces has its appointed hours of culmination and seasons of rule.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate movements and works historically: periods dominated by one force may require corrective influence from the other. Cultural critique should favor restoring balance rather than absolute triumph of one mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different nations contribute distinct elements to humanization
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain nations are 'preëminent and representative' on particular lines (e.g., Hebrews: conduct; Greeks: intellect and beauty; Italians: sense of beauty; Germans: scientific knowing; French: social life and manners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging cultural output, attend to national strengths and specializations rather than applying a single universal standard; recognize contribution rather than reduce a nation's whole value to a single axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social manners (spirit of society) promote equality
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'power of social life and manners' makes men equal: 'It is by the humanity of their manners that men are made equal...A community having humane manners is a community of equals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess social/cultural practices and literature by their contribution to humane manners and conviviality; cultivating manners and social spirit is an effective route to social equality, distinct from philanthropy or abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating a single cultural force as the law of development
rubrics_metrics.description: Hebraism and Hellenism 'are, each of them, contributions to human development' and 'neither of them, the law of human development' though admirers often mistake them for such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique that elevates one mode to the exclusive principle of progress is flawed. Good critical practice recognizes plurality of contributions and resists absolutizing one perspective.
